My understanding of superannuation is that it is a hybrid of US pension plans: part 401(k) and part pension. It differs depending on the country.

That said, this issue has little to do with retirement plans but instead deals with taxable stock sales. When stock options or grants occur, there is a cost basis. Any sales within 365 days are considered regular income and taxed at a higher rate. Longer than that and you get to pay long term capital gains tax (39.6% vs 22.5%). Skipping the fact that I object to ALL income tax because it is coercive theft of personal property, it is obviously advantageous to time one's sales of company stock to maximize tax benefits.

Beyond that, there are regulations of how corporate insiders and controlling persons (owners of 5+% of stock) can sell their shares, and most of that has to do with public disclosure. Smaller shareholders need to know if the bigwigs are dumping stock. These regulations require SEC filings in advance. This means that Google insiders selling stock can be traced by their filings. It is easy to see from the filings if there is a rush to the exits.

If that makes sense, let me add that there are a number of tax-minimization strategies to sell company stock that may entail sales that aren't filed, or that result in filings even though the legitimate selling strategy was put in place years prior.. Among these strategies are pre-paid variable forward contracts, charitable trust transactions, gifting, and a bit more.

The whole point I'm trying to make is that simple tables of stock sale filings isn't necessarily a sign of a trend, as the Q post seems to be suggesting, but rather a "possible" sign of a trend that requires more information than is publicly available in order to draw an informed conclusion.
